summary: Crew Health is an interactive web prototype that helps astronauts understand health changes and coordinate support when communication with Earth is delayed. It brings nine simulated indicators into one dashboard, including heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood and radiation exposure. Personal-baseline comparisons, trend charts and clear status labels help users identify changes that deserve attention. When a sensor disconnects, the interface marks the reading as unknown and explains the missing information. A clickable body map, prevention plan and emergency simulation connect health information with practical next steps. Six replayable scenarios demonstrate sensor failures, symptom reports and crew handoffs. Built for offline use after initial caching, Crew Health explores how crews could maintain health awareness during distant missions. All health data is synthetic, and assessment rules and guidance are illustrative.
details:
Crew Health

Helping astronauts understand health changes and coordinate support far from Earth

An astronaut finishes exercising and feels dizzy. Their wrist sensor has disconnected. The latest heart-rate reading is already several minutes old.

Crew Health makes the missing information visible, explains the concern, and opens a crew handoff.


Explore Crew Health

  • Launch the live prototype · Try the interactive crew health dashboard.
  • Watch the 30-second pitch · Get a quick overview of the problem and our solution.
  • Watch the 3-minute walkthrough · See how Crew Health handles a sensor disconnect, a symptom report, and a crew handoff.
  • View the presentation slides (PDF) · Read the Crew Health overview prepared for judges.
  • Browse the GitHub repository · Explore the source code, synthetic data, and technical documentation.

Our interactive web prototype explores how astronauts can monitor health, understand changing readings and coordinate assistance when communication with Earth is delayed.

The extended demo provides a walkthrough of up to three minutes for local judging.

See the crew’s health at a glance

The dashboard combines simulated readings, personal comparisons, pattern alerts and explanations. All displayed health data is synthetic.

Crew Health brings nine indicators into one interface—heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, estimated mood and radiation exposure.

Steady, Watch and Act now labels pair colour with words and icons. Selecting a reading reveals its source, comparison with the demo baseline and illustrative next steps. Disconnected sensors display Unknown alongside the reason.

A clickable body map connects readings with body systems. Thirty-day trend charts help users explore how values change over a mission.

Follow a concern from detection to crew support

Scenario C shows a reported symptom alongside missing sensor data. The timeline and assessment reasons explain why a crewmate is needed.

Our Live check demonstrates six replayable scenarios covering normal recovery, sensor interruption, symptoms, assistance requests and crew acknowledgement.

In the dizziness scenario, the prototype follows a clear sequence.

  1. Recognise the gap. The current heart rate becomes unknown after the last reading exceeds the demo’s validity window.
  2. Preserve the context. The previous value remains labelled with its time and exercise context.
  3. Respond to the concern. A dizziness report opens a crew handoff.
  4. Explain the assessment. The interface lists the missing information and events behind its response.
  5. Record acknowledgement. A simulated crewmate can respond, updating the handoff state.

Explore the Live check demonstration

Support everyday health routines

The prevention plan brings daily activities together with additional items prompted by patterns in the simulated readings. Progress, XP and streaks encourage engagement with the routine.

A sensor-health panel shows simulated battery levels, connection status and last synchronization times. The Guide introduces NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight and explains the purpose of each indicator.

Mission settings cover a station, spacecraft, rover, Moon base and Mars base. They change the displayed gravity, radiation context and communication delay. An emergency simulation demonstrates situation-specific prompts, a vital-sign summary and simulated crew and ground responses.

Build for interrupted connections

The production application supports offline use after its initial assets have been cached. Browser storage preserves demo interactions between visits.

We considered limited attention, unavailable readings, delayed communication and different mission environments. Text labels accompany status colours, and users can reduce interface motion.

Connect research with transparent demonstration data

NASA Human Research Program resources informed the educational content. NASA exercise references informed the construction of our synthetic heart-rate scenarios.

The repository documents the data, source references and assessment settings. For example, the resting-heart-rate demonstration uses the median of mission days 1–14 as a personal reference. A day-140 reading of 74 bpm, compared with a 62 bpm reference, demonstrates a 19.4% increase and triggers the prototype’s illustrative comparison rule.

All bundled health records are synthetic. The personal-baseline rule, freshness window and alert thresholds are documented demonstration settings.

Read our data methodology and NASA references
Inspect the assessment settings

How we built it

The published prototype uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Motion. GitHub Actions builds the interface and publishes it through GitHub Pages.

The repository includes automated checks comparing calculated assessments with expected outputs for the six scenarios and the resting-heart-rate example.

A separate crew-and-ground application in the repository explores daily self-checks, an attention task, report snapshots and optional cloud storage. Integrating its state with the published interface is a next step.

What comes next

Our intended impact is to help crews notice changes, understand uncertainty and communicate concerns clearly.

The current prototype demonstrates these interactions through simulated sensors and communications. Further development would involve clinical review, validated assessment rules, real device integration, secure crew permissions and testing with representative users.

Development credits

AI tools supported idea exploration, research discovery, implementation, documentation and submission preparation. Claude supported video preparation, and ChatGPT/Codex assisted with repository setup and deployment troubleshooting. Further details are provided in our SI disclosure.
